title: Secret Scanning
summary: Secret scanning is the practice of detecting credentials, API keys, tokens, private keys and other sensitive material that has been committed to source control, embedded in build artifacts, written into logs, or left in configuration files and container layers. It operates in three places: pre-commit or pre-receive hooks that block a secret before it enters history, continuous scanning of repositories and pipelines that catches what got through, and artifact and runtime scanning that finds secrets baked into images or exposed through debug endpoints. Detection usually combines high-confidence provider-specific patterns with entropy heuristics and verification calls that confirm whether a discovered credential is still live. For a practising engineer the critical insight is that a secret written to version control should be treated as disclosed, because rewriting history does not undo the copies already fetched by every clone, fork and CI cache. The response is therefore rotation first, cleanup second, and only then rewriting history if it is worth the disruption. Effective programmes pair scanning with a secrets manager, short-lived credentials issued by workload identity, and pre-commit enforcement so the cheap prevention happens before the leak. The usual failure modes are scanning only the default branch, ignoring pipeline logs and issue attachments, alerting into a channel nobody owns, and treating the problem as solved once a scanner is installed while long-lived static keys remain the primary authentication method.
objectives: You will be able to explain why a credential committed to version control must be treated as disclosed and rotated rather than merely deleted.
You will be able to design a layered detection approach covering pre-commit hooks, repository history, pipeline logs and container images.
You will be able to distinguish high-confidence provider patterns from entropy-based heuristics and assess the false positive cost of each.
You will be able to write an incident runbook for a live credential exposure covering revocation, rotation, scope review and log analysis.
You will be able to evaluate whether an organisation's credential strategy reduces secret sprawl or merely detects it after the fact.
You will be able to identify the blind spots of a scanner that only inspects the default branch of a repository.
